title: Banach-Tarski Paradox
text:
In an article by T. W. Körner in "The Princeton Companion to Mathematics," it is stated that, "The Banach–Tarski paradox states that there is a way of decomposing a three-dimensional ball of unit radius into a finite number of disjoint pieces, then reassembling the pieces to form two balls of unit radius, where “reassembling” means that the pieces are translated and rotated and that they end up still disjoint." In other words, that we can take a unit sphere and split it into a finite number of distinct pieces and re-assemble those pieces (using only rigid translations) into two spheres that are also of unit radius. This is a "paradox" because it counters our basic intuition regarding volume, and that a single sphere has a set volume, and any division of that set volume results in a smaller volume.

History[edit]

The Banach-Tarski paradox originated in 1924 when Polish mathematicians Stefan Banach and Alfred Tarski published a landmark paper that fundamentally challenged human intuition about space and geometry. Their theorem proved that a solid, three-dimensional ball could be split into a finite number of pieces and reassembled, using only rotations and translations, into two identical copies of the original ball. This shocking conclusion relies heavily on the Axiom of Choice, a foundational rule in set theory that allows for the selection of elements from an infinite collection of sets without providing an explicit formula. Because of this axiom, the pieces generated in the decomposition are not standard geometric shapes, but rather infinitely complex, "jagged" clouds of points that lack a well-defined mathematical volume. Because these pieces are non-measurable, the paradox bypasses the standard rules of volume conservation that govern the physical world.

The breakthrough did not happen in a vacuum, as Banach and Tarski built directly upon the insights of earlier mathematicians who were exploring the strange frontiers of set theory. In 1905, Giuseppe Vitali constructed the first example of a non-measurable set, demonstrating for the first time that certain subsets of real numbers simply cannot be assigned a consistent size or volume. Building on Vitali's work, Felix Hausdorff published a major discovery in 1914 known as the Hausdorff paradox. Hausdorff demonstrated a paradoxical decomposition on the surface of a two-dimensional sphere, proving that it could be divided into pieces and manipulated to alter its perceived area.

By combining Hausdorff's use of rotational groups with the Axiom of Choice, Banach and Tarski successfully extended the paradox from the empty shell of a sphere into a solid, three-dimensional object. Their 1924 paper served as both a brilliant mathematical proof and a profound philosophical question regarding the nature of infinity and geometry. It highlighted the bizarre consequences of treating physical space as a mathematical continuum made of infinite points, creating a permanent bridge between abstract set theory and the study of geometric measure.
